key_insight: Strong activation does not prove representation — the paper introduces a causal-testing framework that identifies brain regions that truly represent visual concepts by using targeted interventions and counterfactual stimuli to separate causal signals from correlated cues.
problem_solved: Distinguishes genuine concept representations in the human brain from spurious activations driven by correlated visual or semantic features, overcoming limitations of activation-maximization alone.
method: Use activation-based localization to nominate candidate brain regions that respond to a target concept.
Apply causal interventions (controlled stimulus manipulations and model-based counterfactuals / virtual perturbations) to test whether altering the concept changes region responses.
Quantify causal effect sizes and control for confounds to produce a map of regions with validated causal visual representations.
impact: Provides a principled way to validate which neural signals genuinely encode visual concepts, improving interpretability and alignment between AI vision models and human neurobiology and offering tools for building more robust, causally grounded representations.
visual_elements: Cortical surface map highlighting candidate vs causally validated regions (color-coded).
Side-by-side stimulus examples showing original image and controlled counterfactual edits used for intervention.
Causal diagram contrasting a direct representation pathway versus confounded activation by correlated features.
Bar/violin chart comparing activation magnitude versus measured causal effect for multiple brain regions.
paper_title: From Activation to Causality: Discovery of Causal Visual Representations in the Human Brain
paper_authors: Yuval Golbari, Navve Wasserman, Matias Cosarinsky, Roman Beliy, Aude Oliva
